segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The 1960s were a fervent decade for Latin American cinema, led by Cinema Novo in Brazil.
segments.text: The nineteen sixties were a fervent decade for Latin American cinema, led by Cinema Novo in Brazil.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Latin America is a vast and diverse region. Geographically, it covers all the territory stretching from the southern tip of South America to the California border and the Caribbean islands. Politically, in the 1960s it was home to both Brazil's right-wing military government and Cuban communism. In cinema, some of its countries built major industries before and during the 1960s, while others had minimal film production.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The most important national cinema in South America was probably Brazil's. Significant works appeared in Brazilian cinema in the 1930s, but its great leap came in the early 1960s with the flourishing Cinema Novo, a movement whose motto was "an idea in the head and a camera in the hand".

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The most prominent figure of Cinema Novo was writer-director Glauber Rocha (1939-1981), whose best-known film, Antonio das Mortes (1969), is the story of a gunman hired to kill bandits who ends up becoming a revolutionary.

segments.original: Upon attending one of the first screenings of Black God, White Devil, a Brazilian critic reportedly exclaimed: "My God, Eisenstein has been reborn... and he's Brazilian!" Born in Bahia, a Brazilian state known as the cradle of Afro-Brazilian culture, Glauber grew up fascinated by mysticism and American Westerns. In his early twenties, he moved to Rio de Janeiro, where he fell in with a group of young cinephiles who would go on to found the influential Cinema Novo movement.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Influenced by radical politics like so many of his generation, Glauber sought to explore the links between historical change and violence in Black God, White Devil. Here he focuses on examples of popular uprisings in the Brazilian backlands.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Shot in an arid black and white that makes the screen practically shimmer with heat, Black God, White Devil alternates frenetic camera movements with dynamically edited sequences, layering Villa-Lobos's music over wind, screams, and gunshots. The final effect is a sense that the film and the country it portrays are about to explode. Shortly before the film was completed and released commercially, the Brazilian military staged a coup, ushering in a dictatorship that lasted 20 years.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Influenced by Italian Neorealism and the French New Wave, Glauber made his film debut in 1962 with The Turning Wind (1962) and then directed Black God, White Devil (1964), an extraordinary visual study of life in the backlands that combines local legend with music by J. S. Bach and Heitor Villa-Lobos to deliver a harsh critique of survival conditions in the drought-stricken, impoverished Northeast. The 1964 military coup imposed growing difficulties on the Brazilian film industry, to which Glauber responded with the allegorical Entranced Earth (1967).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In contrast to the stylization of Glauber Rocha's films, other Cinema Novo figures opted for a more realistic style. Former documentary director Nelson Pereira dos Santos (b. 1928) made Barren Lives (1963), a harsh account of rural poverty in the desolate landscape of the Northeast. Ruy Guerra (b. 1931) made The Guns (1964), a vigorous study of a group of soldiers tasked with protecting a warehouse from starving peasants.

segments.original: The 1960s also brought Brazilian cinema its most important international award. The Given Word (1962), by Anselmo Duarte (1920-2009) - the story of a small landowner who vows to carry a cross to a distant church if his sick donkey recovers - won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival, and remains to this day the only Brazilian winner of the prestigious prize.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In his 1965 text The Aesthetics of Hunger, Glauber Rocha wrote: "We know - we who made these ugly, sad films, these screaming, desperate films in which reason did not always prevail - that hunger will not be cured by bureaucratic planning and that Technicolor patches do not hide, but rather aggravate, its tumors. Thus, only a culture of hunger, undermining its own structures, can surpass itself qualitatively: and the noblest cultural manifestation of hunger is violence."

Thus, only a culture of hunger, undermining its own structures, can surpass itself qualitatively: and the noblest cultural manifestation of hunger is violence."

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: As the movement's main aesthetic features, lack of resources and creative freedom allowed Cinema Novo filmmakers to challenge, provoke, and surprise audiences. However, this freedom, this abandonment of technical preciousness, made each film an expression of its director's personal vision. For this reason, the movement is not necessarily homogeneous in its aesthetics, since the form and content of the films varied greatly across its different phases.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Cinema Novo was shaped in the image of other movements known for their subversiveness, such as Italian Neorealism and the French New Wave. Like their predecessors, the Brazilians wanted to shoot on small budgets, often on real locations and with nonprofessional actors, addressing themes drawn from the reality of the oppressed classes. A passion for cinema and the desire to use it as a tool for change was what drove them all.

segments.original: For this reason, the movement has no aesthetic unity. The "aesthetics of hunger" itself, developed by Glauber Rocha, dealt more with conceptual issues than with visual or technical ones. The goal was to expose social inequality in Third World countries and to speak of hunger as a symptom of a sick society. As the filmmaker put it: "[…] our greatest misery is that this hunger, though felt, is not understood."

segments.original: Among Buñuel's last Mexican films is El ángel exterminador (The Exterminating Angel, 1962), a chilling parable about a group of people trapped at a dinner party that - inexplicably - no one can leave. segments.original: Apart from Brazil's and Mexico's, the most notable film industry in Latin America was Argentina's. Leopoldo Torre Nilsson (1924-1978) had already won international acclaim in the late 1950s for his melodramatic accounts of the decadent upper class, most notably La casa del ángel (The House of the Angel, 1957), which was screened and awarded at Cannes. The film is based on a novel by Beatriz Guido, co-writer of the screenplay, who would become his wife and regular screenwriter.

segments.original: However, the most important Argentine film movement of the 1960s was a conscious attempt to move away from foreign models. Fernando Solanas (b. 1936) and Octavio Getino (b. 1935) collaborated on La hora de los hornos: Notas y testimonios sobre el neocolonialismo, la violencia y la liberación (The Hour of the Furnaces, 1968). A didactic account of Argentine history and politics, this film became the model for "Third Cinema": a cinema style of its own for the Third World, an alternative to the "First Cinema" of Hollywood and the "Second Cinema" of the new waves.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In 1961, after Cuban leader Fidel Castro nationalized local industries and established ties with the Soviet Union, the United States broke off diplomatic relations, and Castro's regime moved definitively into the Soviet orbit. This new alignment found cinematic expression when Mikhail Kalatozov (1903-1973), the Georgian filmmaker behind the Soviet classic Letyat zhuravli (The Cranes Are Flying, 1957), went to the island to make Soy Cuba (I Am Cuba, 1964). A visually stunning work of propaganda, the film traces the country's path from pre-revolutionary oppression to an idealized, celebratory present.

His later work contains an evolving dialectical social critique: La muerte de un burócrata (Death of a Bureaucrat, 1966) emerged as a surprising satire of the spasms of socialist bureaucracy, while Memorias del subdesarrollo (Memories of Underdevelopment, 1968), a melancholy account of post-revolutionary life, displays remarkable skeptical intelligence for a film produced under a totalitarian regime.
